outcome: Not binned, not passed to a product or security leader, no 15 minutes booked. Dana files it as vendor-adjacent press: the disclosure says in so many words 'This is not independent coverage. We may write about companies the team hopes to meet or sell to', and the three questions on the company page are, word for word, the product lens of RiskMandate, which sells Agent Behaviour Policies in the same space as her company. She checks the facts on the page (nothing wrong), drafts a two-line holding reply for after the summit, and does not offer a spokesperson. She did not stop on any page outright; she slowed hardest at the participant page and finished the rest out of duty.

interview.q1: A summit guide that looks like a newspaper: a page on every company at Web Summit Lisbon, built from public pages, made mostly by AI agents in the last two days. The email is a request for our product and security people to explain where AI agents act in our product.
interview.q2: A small team with three named editors, Dinis Cruz in charge, and a set of AI agents. The same team works on RiskMandate, which sells Agent Behaviour Policies. RiskMandate's logo is in the masthead.
interview.q3: I trust their facts more than most: every line has a source and a date, and they promise dated corrections and no contact details. I do not trust it as press, because their own disclosure says 'This is not independent coverage. We may write about companies the team hopes to meet or sell to.' And I still do not know who reads it.
interview.q4: Nothing urgent. The page is accurate, so there is nothing to correct before the summit. I send two lines in writing after 12 November, and only if they come back with a published article would I look again.
interview.q5: Not binned, not passed on. I would not forward this to a product or security leader: the interview is RiskMandate's product questions about our agents' reach and authority, asked by a team that works on RiskMandate, in our own market. A short written reply from comms, no spokesperson.
interview.q6: Tell me in the email, in one plain line, who reads PrompTugal.news and whether 1Password is a company RiskMandate wants to sell to; if the answer was a real audience and 'no commercial interest in 1Password', I would pass it to someone for two written lines.
interview.q7: Against, from the disclosure page: 'This is not independent coverage. We may write about companies the team hopes to meet or sell to.' For, from the company page: 'If something here is wrong or out of date, we correct it on this page, dated.'

findings.finding: The disclosure says 'This is not independent coverage. We may write about companies the team hopes to meet or sell to', which a communications lead reads as a vendor pitch dressed as press and declines to give an executive's time.

The email's disclosure line 'independent of Web Summit, not of RiskMandate' is softer than the page's 'This is not independent coverage', so the recipient finds the stronger statement only by clicking and feels the email underplayed it.

The email asks for 'how work moves through your product and where AI agents act in it' from a team that works on an agent-security product, and never says whether the company is a sales target, which makes the 15-minute ask read as a discovery call.
Neither About nor the disclosure says who reads PrompTugal.news or how it is funded, so a comms lead cannot answer 'who reads it' for her executives.
The company page says 'We have not asked 1Password yet' while the email asking is already in the company's inbox, because the line is fixed template text.
The sentence 'The team's own notes on each company (why it matters, whether to meet, who owns it)' reveals a CRM-style pipeline to the company being written about and reinforces the sales reading.
The editor who signs the email as 'Vicky Wang, Editor' appears on About only as 'Vicky, editor', while the company page and bylines say 'Vicky Wang'.
The independence bullet and the front-page box open with the bold word 'Independent' before saying the site is not independent of RiskMandate, which reads as overselling.
The '£5.00 credit' in the nav drops to '£4.99' between pages with no line on the page saying whether real money is involved.
The fact 'listed for LIS26 on Web Summit's event partners page (conferenceSlug lis26)' shows a raw data field name to readers.
Bylines such as 'journalist@web-summit.vicky, for Vicky Wang' look like email addresses and leave a reader unsure whether a person wrote the article.
The public footer links 'Synthetic readers' and 'Design review', which make the site look like an unfinished demo to a sender-checking reader.
On the phone the floating 'Ask' button covers the last company names in the related companies list.
On the phone the top nav is cut off after 'AGENDA' at a lone 'N' with no sign that it scrolls.
The 'WHAT THEY DO' description matches the company's own public positioning and gave the comms lead nothing to correct.
Every fact on the company page shows its source URL and the date read, which made the facts credible even when the outlet was not.
'No cookies, no trackers, no account on our side' reassured the reader that clicking the link did not log her as a lead.
The email's 'Drafted by an AI agent, reviewed and sent by me' and the disclosure link in the signature were read as honest and kept the email out of the bin.
